section_summary: This section (pages 37–94) documents proceedings of the Japanese Imperial Diet from January 1931 through June 1932, encompassing the 59th, 60th, 61st, and 62nd sessions. The records—consisting of diplomatic despatches, State Department memoranda, telegrams, and newspaper clippings—detail domestic political turbulence, including the controversy surrounding Baron Shidehara's statements on the London Naval Treaty and the Emperor, tax and social welfare reforms, the incapacitation and subsequent resignation of Prime Minister Hamaguchi, and the formation of the Inukai and Saito cabinets. A central focus is placed on the escalating military crises in Manchuria and Shanghai, debates over emergency war expenditures, diplomatic negotiations with the League of Nations, the United States, and the Soviet Union, and Japanese official declarations concerning the Open Door policy and the creation of Manchukuo.

subfiles.about: Newspaper clipping containing the conclusion of Baron Shidehara's address on foreign affairs and the opening of his address on financial and administrative retrenchment before the Imperial Diet.
subfiles.summary: Clipping of Shidehara's January 22, 1931 speeches: Sino-Japanese relations, Manchurian railways, Chientao, Soviet fisheries and the US Immigration Law, then administrative readjustment and retrenchment as acting Prime Minister.
subfiles.title: Newspaper Clipping of Diet Speeches by Foreign Minister and Acting Prime Minister Shidehara

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch reporting on the reconvening of the 59th Diet session, party conflict between the Minseito and Seiyukai, and Baron Shidehara's controversial slip of the tongue regarding the London Naval Treaty.
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Chargé Eugene H. Dooman reports on the contentious proceedings in the Japanese Diet following the New Year recess. The opposition Seiyukai challenged the constitutional propriety of Baron Shidehara leading the government as Prime Minister ad interim and seized upon an inadvertent remark he made in the Lower House Budget Committee on February 3, where he implied that the Emperor's ratification of the London Naval Treaty testified that national defense was not endangered. The Seiyukai demanded Shidehara's resignation for shifting responsibility onto the Throne, precipitating unprecedented disorder and a legislative deadlock. Dooman analyzes the political inexperience and heavy-handed tactics of the majority Minseito, noting that interpellations on foreign policy remained secondary to the domestic political impasse.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 135: Proceedings and Political Deadlock in the Imperial Diet

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing legislative outcomes of the 59th Diet session based on Despatch No. 191 from Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Memo on the 59th Diet (adjourned March 27, 1931): major social reform bills failed, but 64 laws passed, including poor relief and tax revisions setting land tax at 3.8 percent.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Legislation Passed by the 59th Diet Session

subfiles.about: Comprehensive diplomatic despatch reviewing the enactments of the 59th Diet session, tax revisions, social welfare legislation, and the political crisis resulting from Prime Minister Hamaguchi's illness.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes reviews the 59th session of the Imperial Diet, which closed after a two-day extension necessitated by upper-house resistance to taxation measures. The despatch examines the allocation of naval construction savings resulting from the London Naval Treaty toward tax relief and social programs, including the Poor Relief Law, railway bond issues for the unemployed, and an overhaul of the land tax assessment system established in 1872. Forbes also details the severe political fallout from Prime Minister Hamaguchi's premature return to parliamentary debate following an assassination attempt, the emergence of factional rivalries within the Minseito, Hamaguchi's physical relapse and third operation, and the Cabinet's impending en bloc resignation to make way for Reijiro Wakatsuki.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 191: Review of the 59th Diet Session and Cabinet Crisis

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet and accompanying extract from Despatch No. 192 describing hasty legislative action and the prorogation of the 59th Diet.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 192 extract: the Peers' failure on the Tax Reduction Bill extended the session two days; Hamaguchi was too weak to attend and War Minister Ugaki read the closing edict.
subfiles.title: Document File Note and Extract from Tokyo Despatch No. 192 on the Close of the 59th Diet Session

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing Tokyo Despatch No. 474 and the opening Diet declarations of Prime Minister Inukai and Foreign Minister Yoshizawa.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Memo on Despatch No. 474 (60th Diet, January 21, 1932): Inukai implies defending Japanese interests outranks the Open Door; Yoshizawa blames Chinese-aided anti-Japanese movements but promises equal opportunity.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 474 Transmitting Diet Addresses

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting and analyzing opening policy addresses delivered before the 60th Imperial Diet by Prime Minister Inukai, Foreign Minister Yoshizawa, and Finance Minister Takahashi.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador W. Cameron Forbes transmits and analyzes the opening statements delivered before the 60th Diet on January 21, 1932, by leaders of the newly formed Seiyukai government. In his address, Prime Minister Inukai stresses that Open Door principles in Manchuria must rest upon the preservation of Japanese acquired rights, discusses rural economic distress, and outlines administrative simplification. Foreign Minister Yoshizawa delivers an extensive review of the Manchurian affair, attributing the conflict to Chinese treaty violations, boycotts, and domestic factionalism, while affirming non-territorial ambitions, adherence to the Open Door, and satisfaction with Soviet impartiality. A newspaper clipping provides Finance Minister Takahashi's address detailing the reimposition of the gold embargo, the depletion of foreign specie reserves under the previous ministry, and the necessity of issuing deficit bonds while dropping planned tax increases.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 474: Addresses of Prime Minister Inukai, Foreign Minister Yoshizawa, and Finance Minister Takahashi at the 60th Diet Session

subfiles.about: Inquiry from the American Legation in Peiping asking whether the State Department desires telegraphic transmission of Foreign Minister Yoshizawa's Diet statement.
subfiles.from: Mahlon Fay Perkins, American Legation, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Peiping asks whether State wants the English text of Yoshizawa's roughly 950-word March 22, 1932 Diet statement.
subfiles.title: Peiping Telegram No. 367 Regarding Yoshizawa's Diet Address

subfiles.about: Newspaper clipping providing the full text of Foreign Minister Yoshizawa's address to the special session of the Diet defending Japanese operations in Shanghai and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Clipping with Yoshizawa's March 22, 1932 Diet speech: defends action at Shanghai, calls it a local dispute unfit for League Article 15, notes Manchuria's independence, and affirms the Open Door.
subfiles.title: Newspaper Clipping of Foreign Minister Yoshizawa's Diet Address on Shanghai and Manchuria

subfiles.about: State Department telegram advising the Peiping Legation that transmission of Yoshizawa's speech is unnecessary as it was already published in American newspapers.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: Stimson tells Peiping Yoshizawa's Diet statement was published in American newspapers and need not be radioed.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram No. 92 to Peiping Regarding Yoshizawa's Address

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch reporting on the 61st extraordinary Diet session convened for emergency military appropriations, transmitting addresses by the Foreign Minister and War Minister.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Chargé Edwin L. Neville reports on the 61st extraordinary session of the Imperial Diet (March 18–24, 1932), convened after the Privy Council insisted that additional emergency bond issues for military actions in Shanghai and Manchuria receive parliamentary sanction rather than executive authorization under Article 70 of the Constitution. Neville details initial partisan clashes over the election of the Lower House Speaker, opposition attacks regarding the government's failure to resign after the Sakuradamon incident, and debates concerning political assassinations and foreign policy. Appended to the despatch are translations of Foreign Minister Yoshizawa's Diet address detailing the Shanghai clash and Manchurian developments, along with a Japan Advertiser clipping of War Minister Sadao Araki's speech reviewing army campaigns, logistical hurdles, and the strategic importance of Manchuria to Japanese national defense.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 538: Proceedings of the 61st Extraordinary Diet Session with Speeches of Yoshizawa and Araki

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum detailing an inquiry to the Japanese Embassy regarding the texts of Premier Viscount Saito's speeches before the Diet.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Memo on a call with Mr. Kato: the Embassy lacks Saito's speech as Premier, but Tokyo will mail it, so no cable is needed.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum Regarding Viscount Saito's Diet Speeches

subfiles.about: Telegraphic notice from Tokyo reporting that the full texts of Viscount Saito's Diet speeches were wired to the Japanese Embassy in Washington.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Neville says Saito's Diet speeches as Premier and Foreign Minister were cabled to the Japanese Embassy in Washington, which can supply them.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 148 on Viscount Saito's Diet Speeches

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Peiping Telegram No. 593 regarding the formal opening of the 62nd Diet and Premier Saito's impending address.
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Legation, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Peiping Telegram No. 593: the Diet opened June 1, 1932; Saito expected to address the Shanghai round table conference.
subfiles.title: Document File Note for Peiping Telegram No. 593 on the Opening of the 62nd Diet

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram transmitting news reporting on the opening of the 62nd Diet session and Premier Saito's remarks on the Shanghai dispute.
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Legation, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Johnson relays Nippon Dempo: the 62nd Diet opened June 1 before the Emperor; Saito to cite the May 5 armistice, withdrawal by May 31, and a round table conference.
subfiles.title: Peiping Telegram No. 593 on Opening of the 62nd Diet and Premier Saito's Statement

subfiles.about: Telegraphic inquiry from Peiping asking whether the State Department desires radio transmission of Admiral Saito's Diet statement.
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Legation, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Johnson asks whether the Department wants Saito's June 3, 1932 Diet statement sent by naval radio.
subfiles.title: Peiping Telegram No. 611 Regarding Viscount Saito's Statement

subfiles.about: State Department telegram informing the Peiping Legation that transmission of Saito's statement is not required as the Japanese Ambassador has provided the text.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State, Washington
subfiles.summary: Stimson tells Johnson transmission is unnecessary as Japan's Ambassador already supplied Saito's Foreign Minister address.
subfiles.title: State Department Telegram No. 141 to Peiping Regarding Saito's Statement

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet for Peiping Telegram No. 618 concerning Chinese Foreign Office criticism of Viscount Saito's announcement of support for Manchukuo.
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Legation, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Peiping Telegram No. 618: a Chinese Foreign Office spokesman notes Saito openly announced Japanese backing for Manchukuo.
subfiles.title: Document File Note for Peiping Telegram No. 618 on Chinese Reactions to Saito's Speech
